Subject: Performance SLOs — p95/p99 latency targets (hosted API vs current provider)

Alex / Priya — thanks again for the time earlier. Quick recap from our discovery so we’re aligned and to surface the immediate next steps for the perf qualification: 

- Goal: validate end-to-end p95/p99 latency for the user-facing search UI (token-gen responses + network) and determine whether Redwood hosted API can meet the target vs your current provider.
- Current high level requirements you shared: p95 target ~300ms end-to-end (ideal), p99 target ideally <600–800ms; expected steady concurrency ~40–60 qps, with bursts up to ~120 qps. Many calls use streaming so partial token delivery is important for perceived latency.
- What we need from you to run an apples-to-apples test: a representative prompt set (20–30 prompts with typical sequence lengths), a baseline sample of p95/p99 numbers from your current provider (end-to-end timing), and whether any client-side batching or aggregation is applied.

Next steps I propose:
1) You share the current-provider p95/p99 sample (if you can, attachment or CSV).
2) We provision a short hosted API perf run (2–4 hours) with replayed requests at your target concurrency and streaming enabled. We’ll produce per-route p50/p95/p99 and token-level streaming timings.
3) Based on results we’ll propose either Hosted with SLO guidance or recommend Dedicated capacity if you need strict guarantees.

I’ve attached our hosted latency matrix for typical gen models and a short perf-validation checklist. If that all looks good, I’ll coordinate scheduling and a mutual action plan.

Thanks —
Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.com

Thanks Marissa — helpful recap. A few notes from our side (we pulled the baseline numbers after the call):

- Baseline (current provider, end-to-end as measured in our staging env): p95 = 420 ms, p99 = 780 ms. These include client-to-provider network time and our middleware.
- Our internal requirement: we’d like perceived latency around 300 ms p95 for our search UX; p99 ideally under ~600 ms for critical flows.
- Concurrency profile: steady-state ~50 qps with spikes up to ~120 qps during marketing events. We do stream tokens (server-sent-chunks) for the UI; partial-token delivery matters for perceived responsiveness.
- Other: sequence lengths are typically 150–300 tokens for these prompts.

I attached a small CSV with the sample p95/p99 from our current provider (timestamps + test payload). We’re open to a hosted test first; curious how you handle bursting and autoscaling. Also please include any rate limit considerations for the perf run.

Appreciate it —
Alex Turner
Sr. Product Manager, Finlytics
alex.turner@finlytics.com

Alex — thanks for sharing the baseline. A few clarifications from the infra/hosting side so expectations are aligned before we schedule the run: 

- Hosted API characteristics: for conversational/generation models we commonly see p95 ~90–150 ms and p99 ~220–350 ms for optimized open models under typical seq lengths (<=256 tokens) in our hosted fleet. For longer sequences (150–300 tokens) the figures trend higher; we’ll model your distribution. These numbers are per-token generation + serving runtime; end-to-end will include your network hop — we’ll instrument that in the test.
- Streaming: we fully support token-level streaming (chunked responses). Our telemetry will report first-byte latency (time to first token) and tail latencies separately so you can assess perceived UX improvements.
- Concurrency and burst handling: hosted API autoscaling handles bursts, but for strict SLOs at scale we recommend either Reserved/Dedicated capacity or a performance SL policy (e.g., pre-warmed pools). For your stated burst profile (120 qps) we can run a hosted validation but if sustained we’d propose Dedicated.

Proposed perf validation plan (brief):
1) You provide 20–30 representative prompts + sequence length distribution and a small test key.
2) We run 2 tests: steady-state at 50 qps for 30–60 minutes; burst test peaking at 120 qps for controlled intervals. Streaming enabled.
3) We return per-request p50/p95/p99 (end-to-end with client-proxy), time-to-first-token, token-throughput, and CPU/GPU utilization samples.

If that works I’ll attach our hosted latency matrix and draft the mutual action plan + test script. When you’re ready we’ll schedule a 30m kickoff to lock ramp windows.

- Aditya
